subtopic: CANADIAN ABSTENTION IN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF CHINA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN ABSTENTION IN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF CHINA
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs with reference to the vote in the United Nations last week. Why did the Canadian representatives abstain from voting on the motion to seat the Peoples' Republic of China instead of supporting that motion, as did the representatives of Great Britain and the Scandinavian countries?

subtopic: CANADIAN ABSTENTION IN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF CHINA
speechtext:
My hon. friend has obviously been reading the Globe and Mail this morning in which the same point is made with the same lucidity and precision of my hon. friend's question.
The reason for the abstention was that in adopting the procedure followed last year, this seemed to us the wisest course to pursue in view of our policy, which is that mainland China should be admitted to the United Nations but that Formosa should not be expelled. A resolution was put forward by a number of countries calling for the seating of mainland China and the expulsion of Formosa. We could not agree to the expulsion of Formosa, but this resolution did meet part of our policy, namely that mainland China should be admitted. Because the resolution met part of our policy we therefore abstained. For this reason, and because it rejected another part of our policy, we ourselves did not put forward a resolution: because after canvassing the matter it was clear that a resolution in our terms would not gather much support.
So for the reasons I gave last year and which I reiterated in this house only last week, we followed the course pursued last year. It must be clear that we took the position that mainland China should be admitted to the United Nations.

(3) When in any proceedings referred to in subsection (1) or (2) hereof, any person is convicted of the offence with which he is charged, the court shall, in addition to any other sentence imposed, and after first making inquiry as to the existence and material circumstances of any family or other dependants of the individual in respect of whose death such person has been convicted (hereinafter called the victim), and as to the existence and material circumstances of any family or other dependants of such convicted person and as to 27053-3081

the material assets, if any, of such convicted person, make such order and award for the maintenance of the family or other dependants of the victim out of the assets of the convicted person as to the court shall seem Just and equitable under the circumstances disclosed by such inquiry.
It will be appreciated by the committee, Mr. Chairman, that what I am suggesting in this amendment is this. At the time the court is passing sentence on a criminal convicted of a crime which, but for the passage of this bill, would have subjected him to capital punishment, and which will now subject him to a sentence of life imprisonment, this provision requires the court to make inquiries, first, into the question whether the victim, the murdered person, left any family or other dependants. If so, the court makes inquiry into their circumstances and material assets with a view to establishing whether they are in need of assistance with respect to their proper maintenance.
The second branch of the inquiry would be this: Does the murderer have any family or other dependants and, if so, what are their circumstances? In my view it would not be right or just or equitable to punish the family or dependants of the murderer for an act for which they were not responsible by depriving them of their assets if those assets are limited. The purpose of this branch of the inquiry, therefore, is to find out what are the circumstances and needs of the family of the convicted person.
The third branch of the inquiry is, of course, whether the convicted person has any assets in fact and, if so, what they amount to and whether there is enough over and above the needs of his own family to provide for the needs and maintenance of the family of the victim. Then after making those inquiries the court would be empowered to make such order and award for the maintenance of the family and other dependants of the victim out of the assets of the convicted person as to the court shall seem just and equitable under the circumstances disclosed by that inquiry.
There is room here for the court to exercise proper equity in dividing the assets, if they are sufficient to be capable of division, between the family of the murderer and the family of the victim, or if there are only enough to provide for the family of the murderer and the court does not think it equitable to deprive his children of the means of maintenance, under those circumstances the court will make such order as justice and equity indicate is appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, only two words before the vote on third reading, to say that this bill, which will likely be law in a few minutes, does not reflect the will of the Canadian people at all.
In fact, questionnaires have been sent and referendums held, not only in the province of Quebec, but throughout Canada. I even received letters from people in British Columbia and Alberta, who were opposed to abolition of the death penalty.
At Montreal Expo, where the question "Are you for or against the death penalty?" was put to the public-I understand that some people may have voted twice as we can see on election day in the old political parties-five million and a half said they were in favour of the death penalty while 19,000 only were for its abolition.
The other day, while in the hospital in Montreal, I heard on the radio programs on which the listeners were asked the question and invited to phone in their answer and I did not hear a single one call in and say: I am for the abolition of the death penalty. All, without exception, stated that the death penalty should be maintained in Canada and gave their reasons.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, before this vote is taken, I want to state very clearly that I am against the abolition of the death penalty, in order to respect the opinion of the Canadian people.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING NUMBERS OF SUPREME AND COUNTY COURT JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few brief words on this bill. I support the principal purpose of the bill because I have personal knowledge of the need for the appointment of more judges to the bench in the province of British Columbia as the result of the backlog of court cases which has arisen owing to the increase in the population of British Columbia and other developments.
I must say I have had quite a lengthy experience with and personal knowledge of members of the bench in British Columbia in the supreme court, county courts and magistrate's courts. I think I can properly say that their code of conduct has been of a very high order indeed. While in principle I am opposed to the partisan appointment of persons to the bench, I am not quite sure just what is the best way to correct this.
I should like to give an illustration to point out how fair I found a magistrate to be on one occasion. Along with ten other farmers in my riding I was charged with failure to have a dog licence. We appeared in court before the magistrate. We were all fined $2.50 apiece. After the others had left the court room the magistrate, who had asked me to remain behind, said, "Herbie, you are the president of the B.C. Liberal Association and I am a lifelong member. I was appointed by the Liberal government, but regardless of that the law is the law." He could not deviate from the law. I gave him credit for this.
There have been suggestions that appointments to the bench be made by the Canadian Bar Association. I cannot agree with that. Why should the bar association be given the right to choose such persons? Why should it not be the working people? Why should it not be the small business people or those in other occupations? I cannot agree with the principle that one group in our society should
Judges Act
have the right to make these appointments. I believe we would then have another form of political or partisan appointments because they would be looked at from one point of view. To have persons occupying prominent positions on the bench through appointment by the bar association, the law society, or whatever it is, would be just like asking the grocers in Canada to appoint the men who inspect weights and measures. I believe there would be just as much reason in that.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I am not certain what can be done about this problem. I have heard persons discuss it. Many people are endeavouring to think of another way by which persons might be appointed to the bench. Perhaps the government might appoint a board representing the major segments of our society including lawyers, farmers, trade unionists and businessmen. In this way the government would not be subject to the accusation that it makes political or partisan appointments. In this regard I am not clear about the best thing to do. Let me hasten to say that to date, on the basis of my experience in British Columbia, with very few exceptions those who have been appointed to the bench have served this country well.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING NUMBERS OF SUPREME AND COUNTY COURT JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) would make a statement when introducing this bill. I doubt that many members are opposed to the appointment of more judges. The increase in population is accompanied by an increase in the number of cases and in many provinces court calendars are far behind schedule. In some I understand it takes one, two or even three years before a case comes to trial. The old adage that justice delayed is justice denied certainly applies. One welcomes the increase in the number of judges in certain provinces.
I thought that the Minister of Justice would make a preliminary statement regarding the method of appointing judges because it is most important. I must congratulate the minister on the appointments he has made since assuming his cabinet position. The old criticism that judges were appointed along party lines as party supporters appears to be diminishing. It is my understanding that in one province particularly the minister has crossed party lines by appointing a judge not because of political affiliation but because of ability, merit and experience. The minister is to be congratulated in this regard and I hope he will continue this procedure.

November 30, 1967
Judges Act
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is opposed to the bar association appointing members to the bench. The Canadian Bar Association has taken the position that it should never have the prerogative of appointing members to the bench and that it should always remain with the Minister of Justice. What the association has said is that through a committee of the association they should present nominees for judgeships, which would not be binding on the minister, and that the minister should at least consider those names when deciding whom to appoint. This is a good idea because it removes the matter from the realm of political partisanship such as has prevailed in the past. This has made the job of the judge more difficult when he takes his place on the bench.
The minister is very forward-looking and I thought he would make some suggestion regarding the procedures for the removal of judges. A recent case certainly indicates the necessity for amending the procedures in this regard. It is one thing to have security of tenure but it is another thing when, because of difficulties, a judge should be removed from his position. We should update our machinery in this regard.
My final point relates to the training of judges. Under our Canadian system most judges have experience both as barristers and solicitors but in many cases the weight of their experience is on the solicitor side. When they accept an appointment to the bench they have to deal with many branches of the law in which they are not experienced. It is my hope that the Minister of Justice can devise some system whereby an individual appointed as a judge may sit with a senior judge for a period of time in order to acquire experience in the procedures of every branch before presiding over cases.
Again I welcome the appointment of additional judges. I hope the minister will continue to be forward-looking and will bring about other corrections.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very few remarks to make about the level of pay for judges. Let me point out to those people who point the finger at the level of pay for parliamentary members that the level for judges has been increased twice since the increase in pay for members of parliament some four and a half years ago and exceed it by $9,000 per annum for superior court judges.
Let me raise another point which I have raised previously with the Minister of Justice

(Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell). I refer to what I believe is a discrimination arising in respect of two superior court judges, one in the Northwest Territories and one in the Yukon. Some considerable time ago they received a northern allowance to compensate them for the very high expenses they incur. This is true not only in the case of their regular duties but also to compensate in respect of their non-appointment, similar to their colleagues, to head up various judicial inquiries and commissions. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has advanced the proposition that judges should not be used for these purposes. However, judges are being used and I do not understand why these two judges should be doubly penalized. Anyone who suggests that the justices of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon are receiving sufficient remuneration in comparison with their colleagues in the southern part of Canada should live in the north for a while to find out just what I mean.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING NUMBERS OF SUPREME AND COUNTY COURT JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the provisions of this bill in respect of the appointment of more judges in the province of British Columbia where they are needed because of the great time lapse between a case being set down for trial and actually coming to trial. I feel that I should make one suggestion in this regard. Judges have a responsibility to assure that the matters before them are dealt with as expeditiously as possible. While the administration of our courts is technically a provincial matter, I should like to suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) that in British Columbia, and I assume the same is true of other provinces, the courts take a long two months vacation in the summer, July and August. This is a terribly antiquated and outdated court procedure which should be eliminated as quickly as possible. Except in the case of an emergency, or motions in chambers, the courts do not sit for those two summer months. At that time no case can come to trial. This works a great hardship on the legal profession as well as the litigants involved. It also makes it difficult for judges to schedule their trial work. While the minister has no direct responsibility in this regard, I hope he can encourage the provincial attorneys general to do away with this long vacation. I hope that the judges of British Columbia will also encourage the provincial attorney general to change this procedure of taking long vacations in the summer.

Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the minister was about to get up to speak but he was buttoning his collar button and being unaccustomed to having his collar buttoned he had difficulty in getting up in time. The minister is very avant-garde in this respect and does pretty well.
Some comment has been made about the appointment of judges and the method by which they should be appointed by the minister. It seems that anyone who has taken an interest in politics is now being condemned and relegated to such a position that he cannot occupy a seat on the bench. I think this is quite wrong. I do not think that just because a man has become involved in politics he should be condemned as a potential judge.
I believe this attitude demonstrates a concern that should be very carefully considered. In my opinion it does not matter what political party a person supports. If he has the necessary qualifications he should be appointed to the bench. To suggest, as did the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), that judges should be appointed after special consideration of a list of names submitted by the bar association or the benchers in Ontario would, I think, be a great mistake.
Throughout history butchers have always wanted to have complete command over the appointment of meat inspectors. Gasoline purveyors have always wanted complete control over the inspection of gasoline stations. This is customary. In most provinces the bar association is really a very tight union for the protection of lawyers, although it is alwavs supposed-and this idea is promoted -that it is really for the protection of the public.
I recall getting into a bit of an argument at one time with the Upper Canada Law Society in connection with searching titles and conveyancing. I was then representing an insurance company which was quite willing to guarantee all the titles in Canada at a very nominal fee. This would have meant that anyone selling or buying a house would not need a lawyer. You would be amazed at the great controversy this brought on because, after all, lawyers charge $250 for their services in the sale or purchase of a house. This is the bread and butter of the profession. But this was not the reason given by the law society; the reason given was that what they did was for the protection of the public.
Judges Act
Pav little heed, Mr. Minister, to the urgings of the law societies. If you want an opinion I suggest that the judges now sitting on the bench can give you a very accurate summary of the nominees you have. After all, they have heard them plead cases and pretty well know what sort of a judge a person will make. A judge must be a person who has a great respect for the law. This is essential. I suggest that the minister would do much better in this field if he took notice of their ideas with respect to nominations.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on some of the remarks made by hon. members, mainly concerning the appointment of judges. I did not stand up to speak first on second reading, though I was prepared to do so if no one else had risen. When I saw hon. members were rising I preferred to let them speak first. As a matter of fact, I thought they would congratulate me on the way in which I have been appo;nting judges. In fact, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) did have some very kind words to say. I want to clear up the matter of the appointment of judges because hon. members seem to be unaware of the procedure I have been following. I have publicly stated what this procedure is.
Hon. members know that practically every year since 1952 the question of amending the Judges Act has come before the house. Reading some of the past debates I have seen that generally the minister of justice, at least this was the case last year, has been strongly urged by various hon. members to consult some sort of committee before appointing judges or, rather, recommending that the governor in council appoint them. In fact, at the meeting last September of the Canadian Bar Association I sat in at a press conference given by the president of the judicial nominations committee of the association. At that press conference, which obviously did not receive the attention of the members of this house, it was stated that it has been my practice since becoming minister to consult with the president, and through him with the

November 30, 1967
Judges Act
members of that committee of the Canadian Bar Association, before appointing any judge.
I think I can say that without exception, to my knowledge and memory, I have not appointed a single judge since becoming minister without having at least asked the opinion of this committee. I stated at that time that this was as far as I intended to go then. I wanted to try out this mechanism personally before committing the government to it officially. I was doing it on a trial basis. I must say, incidentally, that as far as I am concerned it has worked very well. The members of this committee have been extremely helpful to me in making sure that any person I have named at least did not have a black mark against him with the bar. Again, to the best of my memory, I have made no appointment of a person which had met with the disapproval of this committee.
That does not mean I am bound to continue in this direction. I think the law on this point is well understood by hon. members. The governor in council has the responsibility for nominating judges. This is the way I think it should remain. The hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) used some very good metaphors indicating why this should be the practice. I think it is quite right that the people responsible to the citizens of this country should in the final analysis make the nominations and bear the blame if their nominations are bad.
I do not agree that a committee should submit a list of names to the Minister of Justice in order that he may choose judges to be appointed. In this regard I do not agree with some of the suggestions, made constructively I am sure, by some of the members of the New Democratic party. My policy is not to choose a judge from a list of names submitted to me. My policy is to go to this particular committee of the Canadian Bar Association and say:	I am thinking of
appointing so-and-so; I should like to know whether in your opinion he is qualified.
I think this is the only proper procedure under the constitution. I should not be limited in any way as to the names I should consider. Even if I did not agree with the recommendation of the Canadian Bar Association I would feel free to proceed with the nomination anyhow. But in fact I have not made any appointment which did not meet with their approval. As far as I am concerned, this has been a very helpful and constructive procedure. It has permitted me to make sure that I was not choosing people

whom the members of the bar association did not feel were qualified.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
As to the political character of the appointments, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) mentioned that I had made an appointment in one province at least of a person who is not of our political persuasion. He referred to the fact that in one province I had named a person who, rightly or wrongly, has been associated with the hon. member's political party. I think this might be true of other appointments of judges in other provinces who have been associated with a party other than the Liberal party. However, I am not too concerned about the political past of the appointee. If he is a good person and is qualified for the bench, then these are sufficient qualifications and they are the ones that are uppermost in my mind. It has happened on occasion that I discovered post facto that a certain appointee was of such and such a political persuasion, but this is not the most relevant consideration in my choice.
I am very grateful for the contribution which the Canadian Bar Association has made through this committee which, as might be recognized, must be fairly burdensome to them because it is composed of at least one member from each province and in some cases of more than one. The committee is rather large and the members consult among themselves. I believe they do it with as much secrecy as possible. I am very grateful for their help in that regard.
While I am on my feet I should like to touch on one or two other matters which were raised. First, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) commented on the increase in judges' salaries. I am not quite certain whether I understood him correctly but in case I did I should like to set the facts straight. Under this bill no increase in salaries has been provided.

I will gladly answer the question. What happens in fact, as the hon. member well knows, is that this is an area where the jurisdiction is divided. In each of the cases in which I have recommended an increase in the number of judges I have only done so after having received the advice of the attorneys general of the provinces concerned with regard to a new opening. I did not make new appointments until such a request was made.
Each of the provinces seeking the appointment of additional judges has, over the past year, amended its law. These laws bear various names but all of them have to do with the administration of justice, and during the past year they have asked that provision be made in the federal law for the salaries of additional judges. Of course, under our constitution the provinces decide on the number of judges necessary to administer justice, and under section 96 the federal government appoints these judges and provides for their salaries.
This reminds me of a point made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) who spoke about the long vacations enjoyed by judges. He said quite correctly that this matter was not under my jurisdiction, although under the Judges Act the Minister of Justice must give permission to a judge if he is to be absent for more than 30 days. However, the provision of vacations for the courts in the various provinces is determined by the provincial governments. I will certainly consider the matter raised by the hon. member and although I would not presume to tell the provinces how they should administer justice I will gladly raise this point informally when I have the occasion to meet the provincial attorneys general.

judges. I can only speak for my own province in that regard but I should like to say that the chief justices in the various courts in my province have been most co-operative and have always arranged for a judge to be on duty during July and August. This is not a holiday for them. During the summer they have an opportunity to write their reserved judgments and to catch up on their work.
I should like to be fair to the courts in that regard and say that so far as Alberta is concerned I have always found, and other lawyers from that province will confirm what I say, that there has always been a judge on duty during the summer vacation. In fact sometimes during July and August justice is administered more expeditiously because at that time it is possible to go directly to the court clerk at a moment's notice. I was glad to hear the Minister of Justice say that he would speak to the attorneys general about this matter. I am well aware of the fact that in this regard provincial legislation comes first and that federal jurisdiction comes next but the federal government pays the bills and therefore we are responsible when legislation is passed.
There is one further point I should like to make. I agree that it is a good idea to receive guidance from the law societies. I have nothing but respect for our law associations but it must be admitted that there are politics in every organization. It may not be of the same variety as the politics exercised here but nevertheless it exists.
I agree with the hon. member who said that the fact that a man has served in public life should not disqualify him for an appointment to the bench. In this connection I should like to refer with some respect to a former member of the house who is now deceased but who was a judge of both the Queen's Bench division and the court of appeal in Saskatchewan. I refer to the late Judge McNiven who was one of the finest judges we have had. Not only was he highly qualified but his experience in public life and in dealing with people added to his humane approach as a judge. So it does not seem to me that the fact that a man has served in a provincial legislature, in the House of Commons, or in public affairs should in any way debar him from appointment to the bench. Such service should be taken into consideration by the Minister of Justice because if a man has received the approval of his peers at home we can be certain that he will make a good judge and will be humane in making

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. The purpose of this statement is to present to the house the fiscal measures which the government considers necessary at this time to achieve three urgent, and closely related objectives: first, to restrain the inflationary increases in prices, costs and the cost-of-living that are undermining our prosperity; second, to ease the disturbing strains in the capital market that threaten our continued economic growth; and third, to meet in a non-inflationary way the costs of continuing public programs essential to social security and long-run national development.
I might recall that in my speech introducing the budget of June 1st, which is still before the committee of ways and means, I noted that our budget policy was to assist in the transition from the rapid economic
The Budget-Mr. Sharp expansion of recent years to a steady growth in employment and production at levels near capacity. Our budget was therefore intended to exert a moderate sustaining force upon the economy. It provided for a deficit of about $300 million in terms of our national economic accounts, excluding operations of the Canada Pension Plan. Tax reductions proposed in that budget were designed to contribute to a decrease in certain key prices, particularly those of machinery and equipment in order to improve industrial efficiency, and in those of drugs, to relieve the group of consumers in the country most deserving of such assistance.
The budget involved over-all net cash requirements for the current fiscal year of $1,590 million, to be financed by borrowing and by the reduction of our cash balances. These high financial requirements were due not only to the deficit in our budget accounts, which was forecast at $740 million, but also to a large volume of government loans and investments, particularly for house building. The housing loans were intended to bring and did bring a recovery in house building from the low levels to which it fell last year as a result of the severe competition for funds from other borrowers.
On October 4th I made a second statement in the budget debate. In it I said that the outlook for production and employment this year was much as expected at the beginning of June. There were, however, two major problems. The first was the continued high rates of increase in costs of production and in prices. These increases were much too high. The second problem was the very disturbed state of the capital markets, where high and rising interest rates continued to prevail in Canada, as in other major western countries, despite a substantial rate of expansion in the money supply. I said that the expectation by investors of continued inflation was contributing to this extraordinary condition of the capital markets. We had to find some way of bringing the inflationary movement under control. This would require the exercise of restraint on increases in prices, wages, other money incomes such as rent and dividends, and government expenditures. I noted that the government, in preparing next year's expenditure estimates, was making an early and extraordinary effort to limit the growth in its spending programs and its demands on the capital markets.
On the 10th of this month I announced in the house that our budgetary expenditure programs for next year would be held to

November 30, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Sharp $10,300 million. This would be apart from medicare which would be financed by new revenue raised for the purpose, and the writing off of the Expo deficit in our accounts which does not represent any new disbursement. By this action, by the reductions in our lending programs, and by some tax measures, we would hold our overall net cash requirements and our consequent demands on the capital market in the next fiscal year to less than $750 million, apart from unforeseen requirements for our foreign exchange reserves.
I stated then, Mr. Speaker, that these various measures would be a part of an integrated program to check the inflation of prices and costs occurring in Canada and to reduce the excessive pressures upon our capital markets. Tonight it is my duty to carry forward the program by reporting more fully on our situation and on the government's intentions, and to propose those tax measures we consider necessary.
Economic Situation
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)

First, I will note briefly the economic situation and prospects, though these are not substantially different to what they were when I spoke in October.
During 1967 there has been a deceleration in the rapid economic expansion which took place in the last few years. Our gross national product has nevertheless continued to expand, and for this year I expect the increase will turn out to be approximately 7 per cent. In terms of volume, however, the increase will be less than half of this, as prices have continued to increase at excessive rates. The expenditures of consumers, supported as they are by rising wages and salaries, are at a high and increasing level. The expenditures of governments and municipalities on goods and services continue to rise this year although not as rapidly as heretofore. In the first half of 1967, exports reached a record level, although in recent months they have been declining, both in the case of wheat and, to a lesser degree, in the total excluding wheat. This has of course reflected to some extent the slowdown in expansion in the United States and overseas as well as the special circumstances of the wheat market. For the year as a whole, however, exports will reach the target set by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters). Business capital expenditures have also been declining in recent months, both on construction and on machinery and equipment.

The result of these recent changes in the sustaining forces in the economy has been a slowing down in the rate of growth of production, a slight downturn in total employment, and a rise last month in unemployment. The economy has ceased to be under the serious strain it experienced last year, and has developed a small amount of spare capacity.
These developments, however, have not put a check on prices and costs; the excessive rates of increase in wages and in other costs continue unabated. The consumer price index has declined fractionally during the past two months, chiefly because food prices fell as they normally do at this season. Still, the underlying movement remains strongly upward. Excluding food, the consumer price index is up by 4J per cent over a year ago. Costs have been rising rapidly and profits have been squeezed. Our most comprehensive measure of prices-the price component of the gross national product-showed an increase in the second quarter of this year of 5 per cent over the second quarter of 1966.
Canada is now finding it harder to achieve price stability and full employment at the same time than earlier thinking had led us to suppose. Even with unemployment at levels we do not regard as satisfactory, prices and wages are rising too rapidly. They are rising more rapidly than those in the United States, more rapidly than those in most other western industrialized countries. No group in Canada can afford this erosion of our international competitive position.
Moreover, and even more important, the expectation that prices and costs will continue to rise is creating an inflationary psychology which is having serious effects on both the capital market and the labour market. In the labour market this psychology is leading to continued demands for wage increases that are clearly far in excess of any prospective increase in productivity, and therefore clearly inflationary. Increases in major wage settlements negotiated in Canada over the first nine months of this year are reported by the Department of Labour to have averaged 8.7 per cent a year over the life of the agreements. A roughly comparable average for the United States is 4.4 per cent per year. In the capital market the same psychology is leading to an unwillingness to lend money for long terms on bonds and mortgages except at very high interest rates.
Both the labour and the capital markets must work efficiently if we are to continue to be prosperous and to develop our economy.
November 30, 1967

In particular we are a nation which must save and invest about one-fifth of our total national output each year, mainly through the medium of the capital market. In addition we expect to obtain a net annual inflow of capital of nearly a billion dollars or more. We run our economy on the basis of such expectations, and this continued flow of savings and investment is essential to the productive employment of our growing labour force. It is vital therefore that our capital market continue to work effectively and in a proper relationship to the central capital market of the world, which is in the United States.

November 30, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Sharp meantime the government is having to make the basic decisions which will be reflected there, along with those expenditures arising out of statutes. It is essential that the house and the public recognize the nature and severity of the problem that confronts us and the need to cope with it.
Since this government took office it has been putting into place, as it stated it would, the major reforms required to complete Canada's social security system. On our recommendation, parliament has also authorized a substantial increase in the contributions to what is now Canada's first priority, higher education. This was done both in the form of expenditures and in the form of a special fiscal transfer to the provinces for this purpose. We have deliberately transferred to the provincial governments additional resources so that they and their municipalities could provide the rapidly expanding services required of them. We have pressed forward with measures to promote scientific research, industrial development, and the improvement of those areas in the country which have suffered from slower growth and lower incomes than elsewhere.
We made no secret of the fact-and the house was aware-that all these reforms would involve substantial increases in public expenditures. Indeed, we were urged to go even further. I made it quite clear last year and this year that the requirements of a growing and developing Canada in which these economic and social reforms were proceeding would involve increased claims by governments and their agencies on the national output. Even so, I pointed out the growth in the public sector of our economy was not going to be so rapid as to require more than a portion of the growth in the national output as a whole, although it would and did involve higher tax rates.
Let me illustrate. In the last fiscal year our total federal government expenditure on the comprehensive basis used in the national economic accounts amounted to $9,846 million, which was 16.8 per cent of the gross national product. Five years before, in 1961-62, when the party opposite was in office, it was 19.2 per_cent of the . gross national product, and five years before that again, in 1956-57, the totaTwas $5,126 million, which was 16.4 per cent of the gross national product.. Thus it will be seen that although our expenditures over the same decade had increased by 92 per cent, they were about the same share of the gross national product as they were ten years ago, and a smaller share than they
[Mr. Sharp.l
were five years ago... Moreover, during this penod"we reduced our tax rates in favour of the provinces, as I mentioned a moment ago. In addition, parliament has during this period enacted the Canada Pension Plan which is not reflected in these figures. It is a separate, fully contributory, funded plan in which at this early stage the contributions far exceed the payments and produce a large investment fund which is placed at the disposal of the provincial governments to help them meet their capital requirements. Now let me look at the expenditures of provincial governments and municipalities.
The expenditures of provincial governments and municipalities have been rising much more rapidly over this past decade than those of the federal government. Again using the figures as produced for the national economic accounts, provincial and municipal expenditures together show a total in the last fiscal year of $10,942 million, which was 18.6 per cent of the gross national product. Five years before that, in 1961-62, they were 16.3 per cent of the gross national product, and five years before that again, in 1956-57, they were $3,474 million, which was 11.1 per cent of the gross national product. In other words, in contrast with federal government expenditures which have maintained a constant proportion over the last ten years, provincial and municipal expenditures between them have risen from 11.1 per cent to 18.6 per cent of the gross national product. The average annual growth rate over this period of provincial plus municipal expenditures has been 12.1 per cent as compared with the average growth rate in federal expenditures of 6.7 per cent. I should add here that the federal expenditures I have given include contributions to the provinces and municipalities which would have to be eliminated before one added the figures to get a total, since the provincial and municipal figures include expenditures made from monies received from federal sources.	^
While it will be noted that these rates of increase of provincial and municipal expenditures have been substantially greater than our own, I am not criticizing the provinces in any way for this. It is well known that many of the increasing demands for public facilities and public services arising from the rapid growth of our population, our labour force, and our economy generally, as well as from the shift of population from the rural to the urban areas, fall upon provincial governments and their municipalities. This is a fact of life which must be taken into account in
November 30, 1967

evaluating the rate of increase in government expenditures as a whole.
In appraising the situation this year, and taking into account our various commitments including medicare, the government decided it would have to impose much more severe limits on the growth of expenditure than have applied for many years in the past. This restraint is necessary if we are to check the inflationary influences in the economy, reduce our demands upon the capital market, and minimize the increase in taxes. Consequently we decided, as I stated earlier this month, that we would hold the increase in our budgetary expenditures, apart from medicare and the writing off of the Expo deficit, to some 4| per cent, a rate of increase much smaller than in the three previous years. Once this has been achieved and medicare has also been put into effect, then I believe the future growth in our public expenditures can be held to a level which can be met from the increasing revenues resulting from a growing economy without inflationary consequences. There will be many important programs to be pressed forward by the federal government, particularly in the fields of manpower training, research and economic development, but I think they will not involve the rapid, massive increase in expenditures that we have seen in this past decade on the health and social security programs.
To make this transition we must this coming year make a downward adjustment in our spending programs-apart from medicare-from the rapid rates of increase that we have had recently to more sustainable rates of growth, just as we have been endeavoring in the past 18 months to adjust our rates of economic expansion. This will not be easy. To some it may appear at first blush that the ceiling on budgetary expenditures next year of $10,300 million-which allows an increase in the neighbourhood of $400 million over the revised forecast of this year's expenditure-is not a difficult one to meet. Indeed, I have seen comments like this in the press, that submit we are not setting ourselves a very difficult target. In fact it means that over large areas of the government's operations we will be wielding the axe.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Let me illustrate. We make a large number of substantial transfer payments to the provinces and municipalities, such as equalization
The Budget-Mr. Sharp payments, hospital insurance, aid for education and the Canada assistance social welfare plan, most of which increase automatically under statute or agreement with the provinces. We have in addition (apart from old age security which is financed separately) major programs consisting of transfer payments to persons, including family and youth allowances, veterans' pensions, and adult training allowances. All of these are also mainly fixed by population factors and by statute. Finally, there are the public debt charges which will inevitably rise if we assume that interest rates will remain at present levels. Taken together, these expenditures require unavoidable expenditure increases of something over half of the total increase of about $400 million to which we are holding.
When expenditures in these categories are deducted from the total forecast for this year, it leaves about $5,640 million of other expenditures which can increase only 3.3 per cent within the ceiling set for next year-a margin which will largely be required to meet the increased costs of higher pay rates and prices.
In the face of these unavoidable increases in our payments to provinces, in payments to individuals under statutory programs, and in public debt charges, and the increase in pay and prices, it is clear that our other expenditure programs as a whole, under our normal budgetary control, will have to be restrained severely next year. The reductions must be large enough to make way for a number of new things that we will have to undertake, such as the program in Cape Breton. I am thinking about the Cape Breton Development Corporation, the Atlantic Development Board expenditures, and so on. Consequently we are going to have to cut back or cut out a number of things that we have been doing. Some programs that we have been carrying on for years will be dropped, some major construction projects will be postponed, some subsidies will be reduced, some expansion of programs-including some the government has promised-will be held back. In planning our programs we are taking account of the greater unemployment in the Eastern areas of Canada and the fact that expenditures there are less likely to be inflationary than they are in Canada generally.
My colleague the President of the Treasury Board, who is in charge of this expenditure control program, will speak in the budget debate next week and give the house some of

November 30, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Sharp the detailed decisions on these cuts. I expect he will deal with the plans for restraining the growth of the public service, about which many people have expressed concern. I would make only one point about that to keep the subject in perspective. It is that the size of the federal Public Service has for the past 15 years-whether there were ceilings on or off-remained very close to one per cent of the population of Canada and for the past half dozen years has been declining as a percentage of the Canadian labour force.
I have seen suggestions, and probably will hear some suggestions that we should be cutting back government expenditures. I am sure I have the support of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in saying that this is unrealistic, because I have here a report of an interview with the Leader of the Opposition which appears in the most recent issue of Executive Magazine, in which he says:
I think anybody who suggests that you can cut down on government spending or offer a substantial reduction in taxes isn't being very realistic. But any government can control the rate of the increase in expenditure.

speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition can try to convince us that our rate increase is too high, but all he was able to do was increase the last increase, and his last increase was much greater than ours.
Government Lending Programs
Our problem in regard to the demands we make on the capital market arises, as I have indicated, not only from our spending programs but also to a large extent from our lending programs. In the current fiscal year for example, we are lending from the treasury to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing and related purposes a net amount of $608 million, after taking into account repayments we receive. We are lending to the Farm Credit Corporation for farm mortgages a net amount of $167 million. We are advancing to the Veterans Loan Board for housing and farm credit purposes $60 million. The size of these lending programs will have to be restricted. I am confident we can do this without serious economic effects, when account is taken of the better flow of mortgage funds we can now expect the capital market to provide.
Another demand upon our funds is Air Canada. It is having to expand rapidly its

fleet of aircraft and its various ground installations in order to meet the growing traffic demands on it. The Minister of Transport and I recognize that it will be necessary to exercise restraint on what the government lends to Air Canada in future years, requiring that company to seek sources of capital funds other than the govermnent. On the other hand, two of our large lending programs will come to an end in 1968, that for Expo and that for the Municipal Development and Loan Board, and we can expect some recoveries in future of what we have lent under both these categories.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the government is applying rigorous restraints on its spending and lending as part of our program to check the inflation of prices and costs, to reduce excessive pressures in our capital markets, and to minimize increase in taxes.
Budgetary Outlook and Policy
Given the situation I have described, we have come to the conclusion that some increases in taxes are essential in order to meet our growing expenditures even under the restraints we have imposed, and to reduce our over-all cash requirements to what we can reasonably expect to finance in the market. Our large cash balances of last April were down to rock bottom at the beginning of this month. Fortunately the Canada savings bond campaign has succeeded in raising a substantial amount of new cash during November, despite the very adverse circumstances under which it had to be carried on. I wish to take this opportunity to express my admiration and gratitude to those who have organized and carried out this campaign this year. We will need to come frequently to the market in the next sixteen months, both for refunding and for cash. We face an unusually large maturity of savings bonds in 1968, and will consider making an offer to holders of these bonds to convert them into a new issue of savings bonds in advance of their maturity on November 1st. I feel we must ensure that our over-all cash requirements, apart from the effects of unforeseen changes in our exchange reserves, should be kept well within our $750 million limit for 1968-69.
To attain this objective is going to require the virtual elimination of our budgetary deficit next year. This is because, even after the reductions proposed in our lending program, our net non-budgetary requirements next year will be large, including as they should some repayment of the 1966 refundable tax
November 30, 1067

on corporate cash flows. In addition it is important to build up our cash balances from the low levels they are likely to be at in March 1968.
Our budgetary expenditures in the current fiscal year-this year-are now expected to be about $9,900 million. Our revenues, before taking into account tax changes I am proposing tonight, are likely to amount to about $9,070 million. Although these figures are different from my June budget forecast, I intend that our tax and expenditure measures will hold the budgetary deficit as close as possible to what was planned at that time. It now appears that our over-all cash requirements for the year as a whole-apart from the refunding of our debt and on the basis of the current level of our exchange reserves -will be about what I expected in the budget speech of June.
Outlook for 1968-69
The best preliminary forecast I can make of the yield next fiscal year of our revenues under our current tax laws-which of course at this early date is more uncertain than is usual in normal springtime budgets, is about $9,700 million. With our expenditures at the level of $10,300 million where we have decided to hold them, apart from medicare and Expo, our budget deficit would be $600 million. I believe we can and should aim to eliminate most of this deficit.
The fiscal restraints that are essential now may limit somewhat the increase in our production next year but such a limitation now is far better than a serious recession later. If we cannot, as individuals and organizations, exercise the restraint that is now called for in price, cost and wage increases then there is no alternative but a collective fiscal restraint exercised by parliament. This is a case where the proverbial ounce of prevention now is far preferable to a pound of cure later. When the government and parliament have taken the action we should to hold our expenditures in check and to meet our expenditure requirements by tax revenues, then we should, as I said in October, support such action by a determined campaign to achieve by voluntary co-operation a large reduction in the unacceptably high rate at which prices and costs are increasing, including wage settlements.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
We must bring to an end the present round of inflationary price and cost increases, and move to a situation in which all Canadians
The Budget-Mr. Sharp can work and buy and bargain and invest in the expectation that their money over the years will maintain its real value. To the extent that we can mobilize public opinion effectively in support of this objective, and against the actions of those who clearly exploit their market power to obtain inflationary increases, then we can have a higher level of employment, production and incomes along with price stability. This would be, in the words of the Leader of the Opposition, "a more civilized way to control inflation". I think that we can do it. The government is planning to organize a temporary program of this kind-after we have done our part here in parliament to restrain our spending and to impose the taxes necessary to finance, in a non-inflationary way, the expenditures which we in this house have judged to deserve the priority that is implied in our approval of them. When these measures have been approved I would then propose, with several of my colleagues, to initiate discussions with leaders of labour, of management, and other main elements of the economy, as to the manner in which we could most effectively organize this program of restraint.
The Tax Reform Program
Before putting forward my revenue proposals I think it is desirable to say what I can now about our plans in regard to the tax reform program on which we have been working and about the reactions we have received to the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation.
In the first place it must be recognized that our tax reform program must be undertaken under circumstances quite different to those contemplated in the terms of reference of the royal commission and its work. The commission was designing a system to yield a revenue comporable to that of 1964. Clearly we will need a tax system in 1969 and subsequently which will produce more revenues that that of 1964-even after allowing for the growth in our economy since then, and the consequent increase in prices and incomes and in our federal revenues.

speechtext:
On the other hand we can and will take account of the arguments the commission made regarding the relative incidence of the tax on various income and other groups.
In accordance with our invitation to all Canadians to send us their views concerning the commission's report we have received many hundreds of briefs and letters on the subject. Many individuals and groups have talked to me, and to the Minister of National Revenue, and to other ministers and officials about the report and its proposals. I wish to express our appreciation to all the individuals, businesses, trade unions and associations who have given us their views on this difficult and controversial subject.
I have been particularly impressed that four points have played a central role in the public discussion of the report, and in the submissions made to the government. The first is the sweeping extent of the changes recommended by the commission, and the difficulty of predicting the effects that sudden changes of this magnitude would have on the economy and ultimately on the position of various taxpayers. We have encountered this difficulty ourselves. The second point is that the commissioners have suggested for Canada a tax system quite different from that of other countries, and in particular quite different from that of the United States with whom we have an integrated capital market. This could give rise to economic difficulties, as well as to technical problems in drafting an effective law. The third point is somewhat related to the second, although it has connotations in other areas as well. It is that Canada will need to generate and invest a large volume of savings over the next decade in order to carry out the economic growth and development we want, and we shall need to attract substantial amounts of foreign capital to supplement our own savings. Many people feel the commission did not give adequate weight to this consideration in deciding on its recommendations, and I am inclined to agree. The final point is a widespread concern over the regional impact of the commissioners' proposals, particularly those related to the mining and petroleum industries.
Many of the briefs which we have received contain suggestions for modification of the commission's proposals, or alternatives to the commission's proposals. We are now studying these suggestions, in addition to completing

our own work on tax reform and the report of the commission.
The government believes that substantial reform is necessary if its revenues are to be raised as fairly as possible and with a minimum of interference with the proper development and functioning of the Canadian economy. I believe that the report of the royal commission will turn out to have been of great value to the government, to parliament and the people of Canada in helping us all to recognize the deficiencies in our present tax system and to devise sensible ways to reform the system.
However, the work we have done within the government, as well as the analyses we have received from others, leads us to the conclusion that while the reforms we will place before parliament and the public in the form of a White Paper and ultimately in draft legislation will undoubtedly be influenced by the monumental report of the royal commission, they will be more in the nature of reforms of the existing tax structure rather than the adoption of a radically different approach. They will not necessarily be limited to items which the commission has recommended.
In the meantime our current tax proposals must of course be made in a form that relates to our present laws.
Personal Income Surtax
I come now to my tax proposals. My first proposal relates to the personal income tax. I am asking the house to approve a special surtax of 5 per cent of the amount of the basic tax assessed on an individual in excess of $100. This surtax will take effect January 1st and would remain I expect until we have completed the transition to a slower rate of growth of expenditures or until economic and financial conditions call for a change in our fiscal policy.
This change will be made in such a manner as not to affect provincial revenues. As was done in 1965, I propose that the maximum change in tax resulting from this amendment be limited to $600. The surtax is so defined that it will not apply to single persons with incomes of less than $2,000 a year nor to a married man with two children having an income of less than $3,600. Special Refundable Tax
Hon. members will recall that in 1966, as a measure to restrain the boom in capital expenditures then in progress, we introduced a refundable tax on cash profits. Under the law, the payments must be refunded with interest not later than 36 months after they were due, or after they were received if they were late. Clearly it would be difficult to make repayment in in the next few months, but I believe we should not put off the repayment entirely until the last possible date for that would add seriously to the burdens to be faced during the 1969-70 fiscal year. I believe the measure I have proposed in regard to corporation taxes will provide us with enough cash receipts to permit us to repay a substantial amount of the refundable tax during 1968-69.

November 30, 1967

I, too, would like to pay my tribute to St. Andrew's day, or St. Andre's day, as the minister now calls it. I must say that I was very much impressed with that part of his speech which he delivered in Gallic. Having been made aware of the full content of his budget message, taxpayers all across Canada have a very much closer relationship to the "Scots, wha hae wi' Wallace bled". Now it is, "Canadians wha hae for Mitchell bled."
It has become a common thing for the minister to produce these fiscal afterthoughts and having to correct errors in his earlier budget, or to compensate for his failure to predict correctly what was happening in the economy. Last December 19 the minister brought in a so-called mini-budget practically on the eve of Christmas. As we had expected, he increased taxes. Now tonight, roughly a year later, he presents not a mini-budget but a meany-budget. Again, almost on the eve of Christmas, he increases taxes.

Mr. Speaker, when is this complete disregard for the plight of the Canadian taxpayer going to stop? The minister has asked us to place our confidence in his judgment. How good has it been in the past? The following is the minister's statement made last December 19, at the time when he presented his mini-budget, as recorded on page 11332 of Hansard:
My judgment is that the economic expansion now taking place is more in line with the capability of our economy to grow steadily without inflation.
Later on he said:
-I now believe we can expect some moderation in the trend of wage increases and further restraint in pricing policies.
What has happened actually? Consumer prices have risen 3.6 per cent since then. We have inflation, a sagging economy, higher and higher prices, and extraordinary government expenses, mostly non-productive in nature.
The minister has attempted to lay the blame for the present situation on world wide conditions. He said the whole thing was talked over in Rio last autumn. I will wager he did not tell the other ministers of finance the whole story as regards Canada. Subsequently I intend to review in greater detail just how the government has brought us to this precarious situation.
The Budget-Mr. Monteith
First let me admit freely that there is turbulence in the financial and economic community at large. Then I must say that Canada's troubles have been accentuated to a very dangerous point by the complete ineptness of the government in its monetary and fiscal approach to our problems. Never have so many financial statements been made by a government; never have so many warnings been issued; and never has there been such contradiction and deterioration.
Last June we were presented with a budget in which the minister gave his usual reassurances that all was well, except for a possible danger of inflation which he was confident he could manage. On October 4 we had substantially the same message, that all was well, that there were some problems but they were being managed under this government's policies. The minister stuck a pin in his own balloon on November 10 when he had to rise in the house and say that he needed more money.
The sole purpose of this budget is to raise money for the government's extravagant expenditures. Again tonight we have had a lengthy statement containing the minister's exhortations on what we must all do, but no indication of an awakening to reality by the government. Where is the restraint in this budget? The London Economist said the only policy left to this government is restraint. It urges restraint on everyone else but does not practise it. We have had message after message, statement after statement, exhortation after exhortation, and yet the situation continues to deteriorate.
All the government has done tonight is to go to the taxpayer once more and to turn the screw a little tighter. The minister has dressed up that simple operation with a mass of verbal gymnastics. All that can be accomplished by these measures is a further damping down of the economy at a time when a number of indicators are beginning to sag. I will not quote many people this evening, but let me quote John Meyer from this morning's issue of the Montreal Gazette. This is what he said:
It's difficult to Imagine the timing for the budget being less fortuitous than it is. The economy has lost way and is wallowing in the cross currents of indecision.
The public mood is one of weary resentment of government fumbling. The budget itself can offer nothing to inspire. It is, after all, hardly more than the belated correction of a gross miscalculation, or rather a series of gross miscalculations, over the past two years.
4912	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Monteith
The minister has said that next year he will increase his spending by 4.5 per cent, without taking into account medicare, Expo, or old age security. The budget expenditure, he said, will be $10.3 billion. This means we will continue to have inflation and unemployment in a sagging economy.
The government's measures have been unrealistic and haphazard, with the result that we now have uneasiness, lack of confidence and a growing concern about the economy. We in the official opposition, while being as constructive as we possibly can in the face of this government's fiscal inadequacy, are nevertheless conscious of great uneasiness for many reasons, of which I will just mention three or four.
This budgetary statement does nothing to get the economy back on the track of stable growth. It shows no realization of the damaging effects of inflation, and very little intention to discipline and organize government spending. It is obvious that what we have had tonight is simply a device to help finance an unrealistic level of government spending. The minister's inability to curb his colleagues or to persuade the Prime Minister to curb them indicates that the considerations behind the fiscal policy of this government are not economic but political.
It all comes down to one basic fact. The government has grossly overspent. Later I intend to deal in some detail both with the spending record of the government and with its disgraceful record of increasing taxes throughout its term of office. What then do we face because of the government's complete disregard of any sense of thrift or of any trust placed in it by the Canadian people that it will spend their money wisely and carefully? The Liberal government has so overspent that it can no longer use taxation as a measure of fiscal policy. This has put unbelievably severe pressures on any possible monetary control of the economy, and because of loss of confidence it can no longer borrow the required sums without paying exorbitant rates of interest. I refer of course to the sums it requires because of its huge deficit in turn caused by its spendthrift ways.
The government's prime need is cash -cash pure and simple-to pay its bills. We have witnessed a desperate attempt by the minister in the last few months to instil some confidence in investors for Canadian securities. The minister began by saying that in next year's estimates there will be huge savings. How silly can he be, and how naive does he think Canadians are? How could we

DEBATES	November 30, 1967
know what savings will be made next year? No one outside government circles has ever seen the coming year's original estimates. I would think the original estimates for every year since confederation have been cut and frequently slashed before the final figure was presented by the government. Despite all this fancy footwork by the minister, he said that next years spending will be 4.5 per cent above this year's, a year in which spending has been the highest ever. I ask, why? The press across this country is worried, as we have seen in recent weeks and months, and I would like to read a few words out of an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of November 14, 1967, which read as follows:
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Finance Minister Sharp has been sanctimoniously parading a four-and-one-hall per cent increase in government expenditures next year as thrift incorporated.
By this government's standards, 4| per cent is peanuts. But this is 41 per cent on top of 12 per cent last year which in turn was on top of 14 per cent the year before. All Sharp and the government are doing is to slow down the rate of spending which got out of hand years ago.
If the government had said that it was going to reduce its spending by 41 per cent or even keep it the same as last year, the protestations of a return to fiscal responsibility could be taken more seriously.
This is an example, Mr. Speaker, of the majority opinion across Canada today that this government has mismanaged fiscal and monetary affairs.
If I may summarize, Mr. Speaker, fiscal policy-that is, the attempt to control the level of economic activity-has been tossed out of the window. These taxes have nothing to do with the over-all requirements of the Canadian economy. Indeed they may well do a lot of harm to economic activity. The government simply needs money-lots of money -to pay for its extravagances. It cannot borrow any more. Despite this, it still intends to spend more. This present attempt to bolster confidence in Canada's financial policy by raising taxes should have been unnecessary. The required confidence would have been there had the government acted prudently on the matter of expenditure over the past few years.
When this debate is resumed, Mr. Speaker, the minister's so-called message will have been given the most careful attention. I do not intend tonight to delve into his tax changes; certainly there will be plenty said
November 30, 1967

about them next week. May I simply conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that here again we have had another Scrooge budget with which to face Christmas. I suggest that the taxpayer's lament at this time might well be: "I'm dreaming of a white Christmas-bled white by this government".
May I adjourn the debate, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do have a lengthy speech, but since hon. members are in such a good mood I shall not continue at length. I should like to say to hon. gentlemen that this bill has been before the other place and been to a committee in March of this year. It was reported back unamended, and now appears before the house.
This is an interesting bill, dealing with some of our oldest institutions-the National Gallery, which goes back to 1913, and the museums of Canada, which go back to 1842, some four years older than a similar institute, the Smithsonian, in the United States.
The principal purpose of the bill is to bring together under one administration all national museums, including the National Gallery. There is to be set up one board, which is not to be composed of experts but a board of generally cultured people to represent the country. The members of the board may be replaced from time to time, instead of the
4913
Administration of all National Museums board being a sort of self-perpetuating organization as is the case with some boards. The legislation also provides for the setting up of advisory councils of experts in various disciplines. These it is expected will be of assistance to the board.
This situation is somewhat similar to that at the Smithsonian, which as some hon. members may know is a loosely knit series of museums. Some of them are run completely by government appointed officials; others by individuals who have privately made very substantial donations, such as the board of the national gallery in the United States, which has been set up almost completely through Mellon money.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the legislation deals with the National Gallery and the museums. As hon. members know, some new museums have been opened, including one in a temporary home, the Museum for Science, which was opened a week or so ago and is already proving extremely popular. There is also the new aircraft museums. In fact, there are three kinds of museums in existence. All three branches of the museum, together with the gallery will be placed under a single board of trustees and its officers. There will be a senior administrator who will be designated secretary general, and the purpose of designating him is to bring all the administration into one place to relieve people who become directors of the gallery, or of the museums, and who themselves are experts in a great deal of administrative responsibility and routine.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
We think this will lead to savings of money and to a more economical and improved administration. It will free the director of the gallery and directors of the museums, and allow them to devote their full time to the professional development of their museums. We hope that this type of administration will improve the interest in and support of all our national galleries. The legislation will set up a board of trustees to run our galleries. It will set up a single administrative body, with the persons composing it reporting to the under secretary of state.
The provisions of this bill deal with moneys that will be voted by parliament for the purposes of the corporation, through normal estimates and appropriation procedures. The cost of the administration and operational programs of the corporation will be financed and controlled in exactly the same way as if the corporation were a department
November 30, 1967
4914	COMMONS
Administration of All National Museums of government. There is a normal provision for a revolving fund to cover the holding of publications and their sale to the public. We also provide in the bill for two special accounts in the consolidated revenue fund, both of which will be interest bearing and non-lapsing. The first is a purchase account for the acquisition of objects for the collections on the advice of, and with suitable delegation of authority to, individual directors. As hon. members may recall, in times past money has lapsed if it has not been used in a fiscal year. As I say, purchases will be made on the advice of directors, who will assist in these purchases.
The second account is a special trust account which will enable the trustees to accept, if they see fit, and to administer, donations and bequests of any kind, in accordance with the conditions which may be attached to those donations. In the past it has not been possible to accept conditional gifts. For instance, in the past if someone wanted to leave something to Canada but wanted what he left to be kept in a certain part of Canada, or if he wanted the gift to be used for a particular purpose it was not possible to accept it. We hope that now a much wider group of Canadians will have the opportunity to benefit from the national collections.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the bill are to ensure that the national treasures of Canada are preserved, added to and made available to Canadians as a whole. This bill, which has already been scrutinized by members in the other place, deserves speedy passage through this house, and I commend that course to hon. members.

Of these patrons between 75 and 100 are small producers of less than 50,000 lbs. per year. What about the butter industry and the cream producer? Canadian butter production for 1967 has decreased in comparison with 1966. This is directly attributable to the present dairy policy of the government. I understand the dairy commission announced that the limitation of 50,000 lbs. for a producer to be eligible for subsidy in 1968-69 would not apply to cream shippers, and that there would be consultation with proper organizations as to a minimum quantity of cream to be eligible for subsidy next year, c (10:10 p.m.)
This is a very indefinite promise which will not give the cream shippers and the smaller creameries much hope. Does the minister not realize that without the $1.10 subsidy the cream shipper only receives $2.20 per hundredweight for standard 3.5 milk? This is a far cry from the promised $4.75 per hundredweight.
