speakeroldname: Mr. Bruce S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the implication in the hon. member's question is that small producers are now suffering hardship as a result of the minimum quota policy of the Canadian Dairy Commission for the current year ending next March 31 is of course completely wrong. In fact, quite the reverse is the case. When the commission established the principle of limiting the total amount of subsidies to the requirements of the domestic market, and giving each shipper a subsidy quota for the amount of manufacturing milk or cream which he delivered last year, it made one very significant exception. The exception was that if a shipper delivered less than the equivalent of 50,000 pounds of 3.5 per cent milk last year, he was given a subsidy quota of 50,000 pounds for this year. This meant that if a shipper delivered, say,
10.000	pounds last year, he could get a subsidy on deliveries of up to 50,000 pounds this year. This can hardly be regarded as discriminating against the small shipper.
Presumably what the hon. member had in mind in his question was the statement of the Canadian Dairy Commission on April 14 last that it proposed not to issue quotas in 1968-69 to producers who delivered less than
50.000	pounds of milk in 1967-68.
In answer to his question I can say that representations have been received from farm organizations and from dairy groups with respect to this. I can say also that almost without exception they support the principle that there should be some minimum level of production to qualify for a federal dairy subsidy.
In taking this position they agree with the fundamental point that milk and cream production and subsidies must be related to the

needs of the domestic market, and that the available subsidies should be directed to help develop more efficient production units. This of course was the reason why the commission this year gave quotas of 50,000 pounds to those who shipped less than that last year, so that the commission would put no obstacles in their way to reach the minimum volume which it proposed for next year.
There is of course some difference of opinion as to what that minimum quantity should be. The commission itself announced some time ago that the proposed figure of
50,000	pounds of milk would be reviewed with respect to cream shipments. That review is still going on and as soon as possible, after taking into consideration all representations and all the factors involved, a decision will be taken and an announcement made.

HOUSING-MONTREAL-AVAILABILITY OF HABITAT '67 AT EXPO SITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, November 27, I asked the Minister of Labour the following question:
Since there is a certain shortage of housing in Montreal, and since Habitat '61 is almost completely vacant, will the minister state whether C.M.H.C. intend to take over Habitat '67 or whether they would consider making it available to low and middle income families at least on a part time basis?
In reply to this question the Minister of Labour said that he would have to take it as notice. Under ordinary circumstances I would not have pressed the point further, but since I felt action was required immediately I put the question on the agenda for the adjournment debate.
This month there was an article in the Montreal Star written by Charles Lazarus in which he pointed out that out of the 115 completed units at Habitat '67 only 12 to 15 are still rented, and only two of these will be rented for the winter. He also pointed out that while it was originally hoped to rent these apartments after the conclusion of Expo, this proposal was cut back by the government's hope to reduce Expo costs. In his article Mr. Lazarus said:
The decision announced a few weeks ago by Michael Preston, administrator of Habitat for Expo '67, that the $300 to $715 monthly rent scale would be continued after the exhibition, has been suspended pending further action to place the project under the jurisdiction of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
If and when that happens, it is expected that the range of rents will be considerably lower than the $300-$715 scale.
November 30, 1967

Then Mr. Michael Preston was quoted as saying:
The problem ... is that we cannot negotiate leases since we are waiting for some specific decision by the federal government, which is taking over the project.
It is my proposal that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation take over Habitat as quickly as possible and make it available to medium and low income families, especially those families which have been displaced by renewal projects in Little Burgundy, Lower Westmount and elsewhere. Many of these families have been put out of their homes to make way for these projects, and I understand are having difficulty finding new homes at similar rentals. If no one is going to use Habitat, I cannot see why it cannot be made available to some of these people as quickly as possible.
If there is going to be action, Mr. Speaker, I think it should be taken very quickly. Rents could be scaled to incomes and to meet the cost of services and upkeep. Once the urban renewal and public housing projects to which I have referred have been completed, these same families could be moved back into them and Habitat used as originally planned.
Some might say that we cannot use a luxury project like Habitat for this sort of thing, or set the rents as low as I propose, but it seems that it is better to get some rent from this project rather than get none at all. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we are providing housing for families who are now living in deplorable conditions.
In support of my question the Montreal Star in an editorial dated November 29, 1967 had this to say:
-what use could better reflect the whole spirit of Expo, which gave birth to the project?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: HOUSING-MONTREAL-AVAILABILITY OF HABITAT '67 AT EXPO SITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member who has just spoken for having raised this question. It is timely since I realize full well that people have begun asking questions about the future of Habitat, which played such a useful part during Expo '67.
I am sure the hon. member will be interested to know that negotiations are proceeding now with representatives of the city of Montreal, the province of Quebec and the federal government for the disposition of certain Expo assets, including Habitat. These negotiations should be completed very shortly, and it is quite possible-I will not say probable, but it is certainly possible-that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may become responsible for the administration of Habitat '67. If this is the case, it would be the intention of the corporation to make Habitat available for rental, but I am afraid, that having regard to the very substantial investment and also to the expenditures involved in winterizing such units as are not now occupied, they are likely to become available at a high quality rent rather than a rent which would fit in with incomes of people in the lower or middle income brackets.
The three levels of government have very substantial investments in Expo '67 and it was the hope that certain of the facilities provided would be disposed of, or put to reasonable economic use. That therefore should be the objective of C.M.H.C. were that body, as may well be the case, to take over this operation.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.22 p.m.
